summary: Specifies how multiple multicast VPNs or EVPN broadcast domains can share a single point-to-multipoint tunnel using common labels, instead of each needing its own upstream-assigned MPLS label. It updates RFC 6514, RFC 7432, and RFC 7582.

plainLanguage.summary: When a provider carries several customer networks over one multicast tunnel, the router at the sending end gives each network its own MPLS label. The receiving end then has to keep a separate list of labels for every sending router, and the lists grow as the product of the two numbers. RFC 9573 lets the provider agree one label per network across the whole provider network, so the receiving end keeps a single list.

questions: what is the domain wide common block
what is an upstream assigned mpls label
how do mvpn and evpn share a p2mp tunnel
subtitle: How many VPNs and broadcast domains can share one multicast tunnel without every router tracking a million labels.

tldr.problem: When one multicast tunnel carries the traffic of several customer networks, the router at the head of the tunnel picks a separate label for each network. Because every head router picks its own labels, the routers at the far end must keep a table for each head router, and the number of labels reaches the product of the number of head routers and the number of networks.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9573 lets a provider reserve the same block of labels on every router and map each customer network to the same label everywhere, so one table covers them all. It signals this with a DCB flag on the PMSI Tunnel Attribute and with a new Context-Specific Label Space ID extended community, and it also defines how segmented tunnels take labels from per-router blocks.
tldr.outcome: The number of labels an egress router must know falls from the product of routers and networks to the number of networks. The document updates RFC 6514, RFC 7432 and RFC 7582 with the new procedures, and assigns the IANA values for the flag, the extended community sub-type and the label space ID type.

facts.label: DCB flag
facts.value: Bit 47 of the Additional PMSI Tunnel Attribute Flags

today: RFC 9573 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2024, and it has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 6514, RFC 7432 and RFC 7582, and IANA has assigned Bit 47 for the DCB flag, sub-type 0x08 for the Context-Specific Label Space ID Extended Community, and the initial Context-Specific Label Space ID Type registry.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A Multicast VPN (MVPN) can use Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) tunnels, set up by RSVP-TE, Multipoint LDP or PIM, to carry customer multicast traffic across a service provider's backbone. Usually such a tunnel carries the traffic of a single VPN, but procedures exist that let one P2MP tunnel carry the traffic of several VPNs. A tunnel that does so is called an aggregate tunnel. The provider edge router at the head of an aggregate tunnel allocates an upstream-assigned MPLS label for each VPN, and every packet sent on the tunnel carries the label bound to its VPN.

The same arrangement applies to EVPN, where a P2MP tunnel carries the Broadcast, Unknown Unicast or Multicast traffic of several Broadcast Domains. The use of Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER) transport looks the same from the MVPN or EVPN point of view, so this document uses the term aggregate tunnels for both P2MP tunnels and BIER transport.

When an egress provider edge router receives a packet from an aggregate tunnel, it reads the upstream-assigned label and must interpret it in the context of the ingress router that sent the packet. Each ingress router therefore has its own context-specific label space, and the egress router looks the label up in the space belonging to that ingress router.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is about the labels a provider's routers use to forward multicast traffic when one tunnel carries several customer networks. A label is a short number a router uses to decide where to send a packet next. The router at the sending end of the tunnel picks the labels, and the router at the receiving end has to look them up in a list kept for that particular sender.

sections.title: The Label Scaling Problem
sections.content:
The upstream-assigned label procedures can require a very large number of labels. Suppose an MVPN or EVPN deployment has 1001 provider edge routers, each hosting 1000 VPNs or broadcast domains. Each ingress router assigns 1000 labels, and each egress router must be prepared to interpret 1000 labels from each of the ingress routers. Because the ingress routers allocate labels from their own label spaces and do not coordinate with each other, each egress router must be prepared to interpret 1,000,000 upstream-assigned labels, spread across 1000 context-specific label spaces.

The same problem appears with ESI labels used for multihoming. A provider edge router attached to a multihomed Ethernet segment advertises an ESI label in its Ethernet auto-discovery route and imposes it on frames it sends to other routers over a P2MP or BIER tunnel. The receiving router learns from that label that the frame came from the source Ethernet segment, so it does not send the frame out on its local attachment circuit to that segment. The ESI label is upstream assigned from the source router's label space, so the receiving router needs a context-specific label table for each source router. With 1001 routers each attached to 1000 Ethernet segments, each router may have to understand 1,000,000 ESI labels, even when no tunnel aggregation is used at all.

So far, few if any MVPN or EVPN deployments use aggregate tunnels, so this problem has not surfaced. The document expects it to grow, because a single customer in an EVPN may have many broadcast domains and each aggregate tunnel creates state at the intermediate nodes, and because BIER is becoming an attractive and feasible transport for MVPN and EVPN.
sections.plainLanguage: The problem is the size of the lists the receiving routers must keep. With 1001 sending routers and 1000 customer networks each, every receiving router would need to understand 1,000,000 labels. The same count appears for the labels that identify a multihomed Ethernet segment, whether or not tunnels are shared at all.

sections.title: The Domain-Wide Common Block
sections.content:
The number of labels falls sharply if a central entity assigns one label to each VPN, broadcast domain or Ethernet segment and every provider edge router uses that same label for it. The number of labels needed is then just the number of VPNs, broadcast domains and Ethernet segments.

One way to do this is to reserve a portion of the default label space for assignment by a central entity. This reserved portion is the Domain-wide Common Block (DCB) of labels. It works like the identical Segment Routing Global Blocks used on all nodes in RFC 8402. A provider edge router learns by provisioning which label from the DCB corresponds to which of its locally attached VPNs, broadcast domains or Ethernet segments. For example, all routers could reserve the DCB [1000~2000] and be provisioned so that label 1000 maps to VPN 0, label 1001 to VPN 1, and so on, which needs 1000 labels instead of 1,000,000 for 1000 VPNs.

The domain is defined loosely: it includes all the routers that share the same DCB, and it needs to include all the provider edge routers of the MVPN or EVPN. It need not include internal routers, because the labels used for this purpose only rise to the top of the label stack when traffic arrives at the provider edge routers, so internal routers do not have to set aside the same block.

In some deployments a DCB large enough for all the VPNs, broadcast domains and Ethernet segments is impractical. The labels can then be allocated from one or a few context-specific label spaces that do not depend on any single provider edge router. Each such space is identified in the forwarding plane by a label taken from the DCB, which does not need to be large. Each router is provisioned with the label-space-identifying DCB label and the common labels taken from that space. When sending traffic, the ingress router imposes the service labels for the VPN, broadcast domain or Ethernet segment first, then imposes the label-space-identifying DCB label, and the egress router reads that label to know which label space holds the inner label.

The document notes that these VPN, broadcast domain and Ethernet segment labels are similar to the VXLAN Network Identifiers used in VXLANs: allocating a label and telling every router about it is the same kind of operation, and it is especially feasible with controllers.
sections.plainLanguage: The fix is to agree the numbers in advance. A provider reserves the same range of label numbers on every router and maps each customer network to the same number everywhere, so the receiving router keeps one list instead of one list per sender. When the range would be too large, the numbers can be taken from a small number of shared lists, each named by a reserved label that the receiving router reads first.

sections.title: MP2MP Tunnels and Tunnel Segmentation
sections.content:
Multipoint-to-Multipoint tunnels present the same problem and the same fix, with one extra requirement. When MP2MP tunnels are used for an MVPN, the root of the tunnel must allocate and advertise PE Distinguisher Labels. Those labels are assigned from the label space the root uses for its upstream-assigned labels, and this document requires that the PE Distinguisher Labels allocated by a particular node come from the same label space that the node uses to allocate its VPN-identifying labels.

Tunnel segmentation adds a further difficulty. A segmentation point is a node at the boundary between two segmentation regions; it is the egress node for selective tunnels in one region and the ingress node for selective tunnels in the next. Suppose one selective tunnel in region A carries two flows, and in region B the first flow is carried by one tunnel and the second by another. The segmentation point then has to label-switch each flow separately, which means the two routes must signal different labels, and the common per-VPN or per-broadcast-domain DCB label cannot be used for both.

For that case, all provider edge routers can be assigned disjoint blocks of labels from those few context-specific label spaces. Each router then allocates labels for its own segmented selective routes from its own block, for example PE1 from [101~200] and PE2 from [201~300]. The same scheme applies to per-router and per-region routes, where a label is taken from the block of the router that advertises it. Using a per-PMSI label for a per-router route still leaves the original scaling problem, so per-region routes are preferred.

As an alternative, the segmentation point could look up the flow in the VPN or broadcast domain routing table instead of switching on the label alone. That lets the selective routes of one VPN or broadcast domain share the common label, but the label has to differ from the one used for the per-router and per-region routes, and the scaling problem moves from the number of labels to the number of routes in the segmentation point's tables.
sections.plainLanguage: Two situations need extra care. In a tunnel that joins many routers to many routers, the root router must take its extra labels from the same list as its other labels. When a long tunnel is split into segments, a router in the middle may have to send different flows of the same customer network down different tunnels, so it needs a separate label for each of them. Each router is then given its own reserved block of numbers to take those labels from.

sections.title: The Three Label Allocation Methods
sections.content:
Labels can be allocated and advertised in three ways.

First, a central entity allocates the per-VPN, per-broadcast-domain or per-Ethernet-segment labels from the DCB, and the provider edge routers advertise those labels with an indication that they come from the DCB.

Second, a central entity allocates the per-VPN, per-broadcast-domain or per-Ethernet-segment labels from a few common context-specific label spaces and allocates labels from the DCB to identify those spaces. The routers advertise the service labels along with the context-identifying labels.

Third, a central entity assigns disjoint label blocks from a few context-specific label spaces to each router and allocates labels from the DCB to identify those spaces. A router then allocates a label for a segmented selective route from its own block and advertises that label together with the context-identifying label.

The first method is the simplest, but it requires every router to set aside a common block large enough for all the VPNs, broadcast domains and Ethernet segments combined. The third method is needed only for segmented selective tunnels that are set up dynamically. Several of the methods can be used together, depending on the deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: The document sets out three ways to allocate the labels. A central authority can hand out one label per customer network from a block reserved on every router. It can instead keep the labels in a few shared lists and use a reserved label to say which list to read. Or it can cut those lists into blocks and give each router its own block, which is what segmented tunnels need. A provider can mix the three.

sections.title: The Context-Specific Label Space ID Extended Community
sections.content:
The Context-Specific Label Space ID Extended Community is a new Transitive Opaque extended community. Its first octet is 0x03 or 0x43, the second octet is the length 8, the next two octets are an ID-Type field and the last four octets are an ID-Value field.

The ID-Type field is two octets and specifies the type of the label space ID. In this document the ID-Type is 0, which means the ID-Value field holds a label. The ID-Value field is four octets and holds the value of the label space ID; when it is a label, its most significant 20-bit portion carries the label value. IANA has created the Context-Specific Label Space ID Type registry for this field, with 0 assigned to MPLS Label, 1 to 254 unassigned, and 255 reserved.

The document also introduces a DCB flag, Bit 47, in the Additional PMSI Tunnel Attribute Flags BGP extended community defined in RFC 7902. Throughout the document, a route is said to carry a DCB flag when it carries a PMSI Tunnel Attribute whose Flags field has the Extension bit set and also carries the Additional PMSI Tunnel Attribute Flags extended community with the DCB flag set. The extended community itself has been registered with sub-type value 0x08.
sections.plainLanguage: To let a receiving router know which list a label belongs to, the sending router attaches a short piece of extra information to the route. This piece states the type of the identifier and the identifier itself, which for this document is a label number. A separate flag in the route says that the label comes from the common block reserved on every router.

sections.title: Procedures for Sending and Receiving Routes
sections.content:
The procedures in this section may be used when BIER or P2MP or MP2MP tunnel aggregation carries an MVPN or EVPN, or when such tunnels are used with EVPN multihoming. All provider edge routers and segmentation points must support them when they are used.

Each VPN, broadcast domain or Ethernet segment is assigned a label from the DCB or from one of the few context-specific label spaces by a method outside the scope of the document, and every router in that VPN, broadcast domain or Ethernet segment must know the assignment. The Ethernet segment label and the broadcast domain label must come from the same label space, and PE Distinguisher Labels must be allocated from the same label space as well. Where tunnel segmentation is used, each router is also assigned a disjoint label block from one of the few context-specific label spaces, and takes labels for its segmented routes from that block.

When a router originates or re-advertises an x-PMSI or IMET route, the route must carry the DCB flag if and only if the label in its PMSI Tunnel Attribute is assigned from the DCB. If the label comes from one of the few context-specific label spaces, a Context-Specific Label Space ID extended community must be attached to the route, with ID-Type 0 and an ID-Value that is a label allocated from the DCB identifying the space. When sending traffic, the ingress router imposes the DCB label that identifies the space after it imposes the service label, and then imposes the encapsulation for the transport tunnel.

On receipt of an x-PMSI or IMET route carrying a Context-Specific Label Space ID extended community, a router must put an entry in its default MPLS forwarding table that maps the label in the extended community to the matching context-specific label table, and that table is used for the next label lookup on incoming data traffic. It must then place the entry for the label in the PMSI Tunnel Attribute or the ESI Label extended community in the default forwarding table when the route carries the DCB flag, or in the context-specific label table when the extended community is present.

A route must not carry both the DCB flag and the extended community, and a received route with both must be treated as withdrawn. If neither is present, the label in the PMSI Tunnel Attribute or the ESI Label extended community must be treated as the upstream-assigned label from the source router's label space, and the procedures of RFC 6514 and RFC 7432 apply. If a router originates two x-PMSI or IMET routes with the same tunnel, it must make sure that either all of them carry the DCB flag, all of them carry the extended community, none of them carry the DCB flag, or none of them carry the extended community. Otherwise the receiving router must treat the routes as withdrawn.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are all about staying consistent. A route says where its label came from, either the common block or a named shared list, and the sending router has to give the same answer for every route that uses the same tunnel. The receiving router reads that answer, puts the label in the right table, and looks up arriving packets there. If a route mixes the two answers, or if two routes on one tunnel disagree, the receiving router drops them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document allows the three label allocation methods and specifies the matching signalling and procedures. The first method is equivalent to using common Segment Routing Global Blocks from the regular per-platform label space, the second to using common global blocks from a third-party label space, and the third is a variation of the second in which that third-party label space is divided into disjoint blocks for use by different routers. In all three cases a receiving router is able to identify one of the few label forwarding tables to forward incoming labeled traffic with.

The documents this one builds on list no security concerns related to label allocation methods, and this document introduces no new security concerns in this regard.
sections.plainLanguage: The document finds no new security problems in how labels are allocated. All three methods leave the receiving router able to identify which of its few label tables to use, and the documents they build on report no security concerns about label allocation either.
